extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; general readers of John Locke; people redistributing Project Gutenberg eBooks
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on conducting philosophical inquiry and producing intelligible philosophical prose (method, choice of ideas, audience adaptation), plus Project Gutenberg redistribution requirements appended to the eBook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of inquiry (threefold)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, inquire into the original of ideas/notions a man has in his mind; secondly, show what knowledge the understanding has by those ideas and the certainty/evidence/extent of it; thirdly, inquire into the nature and grounds of faith or opinion (assent) and examine the reasons and degrees of assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke sets this as the organizing method for the Essay: investigate origins of ideas; assess what knowledge is possible from them; analyze belief/assent where certainty is absent. Use this ordered approach when examining the nature, certainty, and limits of human knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for plain and intelligible language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the 'learned but frivolous use of uncouth, affected, or unintelligible terms' which obscure truth and hinder philosophy being 'brought into well-bred company and polite conversation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, meaningful words over jargon; make philosophy accessible to ordinary readers; Locke explicitly treats misuse and abuse of language as a major cause of confusion and aims to correct it (see his extended treatment in Book III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'determinate/determined' ideas to 'clear and distinct'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'determinate' (for simple ideas) or 'determined' (for complex ideas) to mean an object in the mind that is perceived there and steadily annexed to a name; an idea so fixed that the name reliably denotes that very object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'determinate' idea: the immediate appearance the mind perceives. A 'determined' complex idea: a specific composition of simple ideas in a set proportion/arrangement. Authors should ensure terms are attached to such determinate ideas to avoid obscurity and dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using terms, have a precise idea and keep name fixed to it
rubrics_metrics.description: When any one uses any term, he may have in his mind a determined idea which he makes it the sign of, and to which he should keep it steadily annexed during that present discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each technical or ordinary term in an argument is consistently used to denote a precise, stable mental object; failure to do so causes 'obscurity and confusion' and fuels disputes arising from indetermined ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt explanation to the intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The Essay was written not for 'those that had already mastered this subject' but for readers who have not sufficiently considered it; make matters 'plain and familiar' to different sorts of readers rather than aiming solely at masters of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor depth, examples, and style to the audience's background: err on the side of clarity for non-specialists, even if specialists find parts tedious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple expressions or extended exposition to aid understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that one may 'dwell long upon the same argument, and expressed it different ways, with a quite different design' to make a new or out-of-the-ordinary notion intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformulate or expand arguments where helpful; some repetition and varied expression are legitimate tools to reach readers with different imaginations and mental habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly humility and readiness to revise opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to 'resign any opinion of my own, than oppose that of another, when truth appears against it'; Locke altered earlier views (e.g., on Liberty and the Will) upon reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments and evidence openly; prioritize truth over consistency with past assertions. A good author signals willingness to correct earlier claims when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the bounds of understanding and avoid overreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Discover the powers and limits of the mind; be cautious in meddling with things beyond comprehension and 'sit down in a quiet ignorance' of matters beyond our capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or arguing, distinguish between matters where knowledge is attainable and where only opinion or conjecture is reasonable; regulate assent accordingly.
